claims: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 is a U.S. federal law regulating the surveillance of foreign powers and agents within the United States.
FISA requires intelligence agencies to obtain warrants from the FISA Court (FISC) to conduct wiretapping, physical searches, and acquire business records.
Warrants under FISA primarily target non-U.S. persons.
FISA was enacted to prevent privacy abuses by the government.
FISA authorizes surveillance to collect foreign intelligence information.
The FISA Court (FISC) is a special court composed of federal judges.
The FISA Court (FISC) reviews government applications for electronic surveillance and search warrants in nonpublic sessions.
Section 702 of FISA allows surveillance of non-Americans located outside the U.S.
Surveillance under Section 702 of non-Americans located outside the U.S. often sweeps up communications of Americans in contact with them.
Critics at the Brennan Center for Justice and ACLU say that Section 702 allows the NSA and FBI to access communications of Americans swept up in such surveillance without a warrant.
The Bureau of Justice Assistance states that the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 establishes procedures for electronic surveillance.
Wikipedia states that FISA was enacted in response to revelations of widespread privacy violations by the federal government under President Richard Nixon.
The National Security Agency states that FISA (Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978) regulates certain types of foreign intelligence collection.
